title: Island colonization and extinction of an insect species revealed by mitochondrial and genome-wide nuclear variation
content:
Abstract
Our understanding of colonization and speciation dynamics within oceanic islands is becoming enriched with the application of evolutionary approaches that focus on population-level sampling within species, or species complexes, and their interrogation with genetic markers. Such studies have revealed otherwise undetectable colonization dynamics involving sequential colonization events by the same species to an island. Secondary contact among such populations may have contrasting evolutionary consequences, from enhancing divergence through reduced hybrid fitness and reinforcement, to the coalescence of differentiated genomes, potentially enhancing evolutionary opportunity through recombination. Using a species complex of endemic weevils on the Canary Islands, here we explore the consequences of sequential colonization dynamics. Specifically, two taxa from distinct islands (Gran Canaria and Tenerife) are known to have colonized a third island (La Palma), with signatures of admixture between them detected within the single taxon recorded for La Palma, suggesting its potential admixed origin. We use genome-wide nuclear data and a demographic modelling approach to test between hypotheses of either (i) a single taxon in La Palma with an admixed genome resulting from the fusion of the two distinct colonizing taxa, or (ii) the existence of a second cryptic species with gene flow between both. Our results reject the starting hypotheses, instead revealing a period of very limited nuclear hybridization between the two founding taxa, followed by extinction of one, but with a lasting signature of its existence through the introgression of its mitochondrial genome into the surviving taxa.
